title: The Works of Dionysius the Areopagite
author: pseudo-dionysius
attributionNote: The corpus is presented as the work of Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian converted by Paul in Acts 17. Since the 6th century it has been recognised as the work of a later writer, probably a Syrian monk of around 500 CE, and is now called Pseudo-Dionysius.
description: The Dionysian corpus is the foundation of Christian mystical theology: On the Divine Names, which thinks God through the names Scripture gives him; the Celestial and Ecclesiastical Hierarchies, which order angels and liturgy in a single ascending scale; the Mystical Theology, a few pages on the God beyond affirmation and denial; and ten letters on prayer, pastors and the hiddenness of God. Its language of hierarchy, deification and the cloud of unknowing shaped Byzantine theology, Aquinas, the medieval English mystics and the whole tradition of apophatic prayer.
historicalContext: The corpus first appears in the early 6th century and was defended as apostolic at a council in 532; its dependence on Proclus was established in the 19th century. John Parker's translation, published at Oxford in 1897, was the first complete English edition of all the works and is the version the archive carries, with the translator's prefaces and notes.
availabilityNote: Complete. The five works of the corpus — the Divine Names, the Mystic Theology, the Letters, the Celestial Hierarchy and the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy — are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one chapter (caput) or letter per chapter. The two volumes' title pages, prefaces, bibliographies and indexes are not part of the work; each chapter label carries the treatise it belongs to.
